summary: Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to the Sun, a small red dwarf 4.2 light-years away. WANDERERS saw it move 55 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026, about 3.43 arcseconds per year, within 11% of Gaia's 3.86. Its brightness stayed steady (-0.03 ± 0.05 mag). That was measured from the star's outer glow because its core is saturated. All 134 SPHEREx points are flagged as too bright, so there is no spectrum. The nearest Gaia star is 3.6 arcseconds from the typed position, but confidence is high: 3 of 3 checks passed.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: It moved 55 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026, about 3.43 arcseconds per year, close to Gaia's 3.86 (11% off). Stars that drift this fast are usually nearby, and Gaia's parallax puts this one 4.2 light-years away. Caveats: the Gaia match is 3.6 arcseconds from the typed position, and all 134 SPHEREx measurements are flagged as too bright. So there's no reliable spectrum, and brightness came from the star's outer glow.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: Some things already make me less sure. All 134 SPHEREx measurements are flagged because Proxima is too bright, so there is no usable spectrum. The brightness check uses only the star's outer glow and has a ±0.05 mag uncertainty. The measured speed is 11% below Gaia's, and the Gaia match is 3.6 arcseconds from the typed position. A bigger speed gap or a bigger offset would worry me more.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE photographed this patch of sky in 2010, and SPHEREx in 2025 and 2026. That 16-year gap is what matters. Over it, Proxima moved about 55 arcseconds, roughly 9 SPHEREx pixels, which is easy to see. In SPHEREx's single year it moves only about 3.4 arcseconds, less than one pixel. One caution: Proxima is too bright for SPHEREx, so all 134 of its SPHEREx measurements are flagged.
